before.title: The causal domain of dependence of a partial Cauchy hypersurface is an open causally convex manifold on which the hypersurface is Cauchy
before.statement:
Let $(W,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$S\subseteq W$ be a **partial Cauchy hypersurface**: a closed, acausal,
edgeless embedded topological hypersurface of codimension one
([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], the edge being defined as
in the cited source). Write $I^\pm(S)$, $J^\pm(S)$ for the chronological and
causal future and past of $S$ in $W$
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]) and let
$$D^\pm(S):=\{p\in W:\ \text{every past- (respectively future-) inextendible causal curve in }W\text{ through }p\text{ meets }S\},\qquad D(S):=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S)$$
be the **causal domains of dependence of $S$ in $W$**. Then:

**(a)** $D(S)$ is open in $W$ and $S\subseteq D(S)$; moreover
$D^\pm(S)\setminus S\subseteq I^\pm(S)$, so every point of $D(S)\setminus S$
lies on one of the two chronological sides of $S$;

**(b)** $D(S)$ is **causally convex**: every causal curve in $W$ whose
endpoints lie in $D(S)$ is contained in $D(S)$;

**(c)** $S$ is a Cauchy set of the open submanifold $(D(S),g|_{D(S)})$: every
causal curve in $D(S)$ that is inextendible in $D(S)$ meets $S$ in exactly one
parameter value.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(W,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let $S\subseteq W$ be a closed acausal edgeless embedded topological hypersurface of codimension one. Here acausality forbids causal relations between distinct points of $S$ as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]; **edgeless** means that no $s\in S$ has the following property: every open neighborhood $U$ of $s$ admits $a\in I^-_U(s)$, $b\in I^+_U(s)$ and a timelike curve in $U$ from $a$ to $b$ avoiding $S$. All curves and inextendibility use [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], so an inextendible end has no point limit in the specified ambient manifold. Define the ambient causal domains by
$$D^+(S)=\{p\in W:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve in }W\text{ through }p\text{ meets }S\},$$
$$D^-(S)=\{p\in W:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve in }W\text{ through }p\text{ meets }S\},\qquad D(S)=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S),$$
as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. Then:

**(a)** $D(S)$ is open, contains $S$, and $D^\pm(S)\setminus S\subseteq I^\pm(S)$.

**(b)** Every causal curve in $W$ with endpoints in $D(S)$ lies in $D(S)$.

**(c)** Every causal curve in the induced open submanifold $D(S)$ which is inextendible there meets $S$ at exactly one parameter value. No smoothness or spacelikeness of the topological hypersurface is required.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, with the
relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$, $J^\pm$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] and the future and past sets of
[[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]]. Then:

**(a) Openness.** For every $x\in M$ the chronological future $I^+(x)$ and
the chronological past $I^-(x)$ are open subsets of $M$.

**(b) The chronological relation is open.** The set
$$\{(x,y)\in M\times M:\ x\ll y\}$$
is open in the product topology of $M\times M$.

**(c) Closure of future and past sets.** Let $F\subseteq M$ be a future set,
that is $I^+(F)\subseteq F$. Then every $q\in\overline F$ satisfies
$I^+(q)\subseteq F$. Dually, if $P$ is a past set ($I^-(P)\subseteq P$) and
$q\in\overline P$, then $I^-(q)\subseteq P$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and the relations $\ll$, $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** if $p\ll q$ and $q\le r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(b)** if $p\le q$ and $q\ll r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(c)** if $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is a future causal curve and there are
$a\le s<t\le b$ such that $\gamma|_{[s,t]}$ is a future timelike curve, then
$\gamma(a)\ll\gamma(b)$;

**(d)** consequently
$$I^+\bigl(J^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega),\qquad I^-\bigl(J^-(\Omega)\bigr)=I^-(\Omega)$$
for every $\Omega\subseteq M$, and dually
$J^+\bigl(I^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega)$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]).
Call a map $x:I\to M$ a **geodesically connectible continuous causal curve**
when it is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]) and for every strictly convex
normal ball $C$ as produced by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]
([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b)) and all
$t_1<t_2$ in $I$ with $x([t_1,t_2])\subseteq C$, the endpoints $x(t_1)$ and
$x(t_2)$ are joined by a future causal geodesic whose image is contained in
$C$. Write $\le$ for the causal relation of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] (defined by locally absolutely
continuous future causal curves) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat .$$

**(a) Absolutely continuous implies connectible.** Every future causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve.

**(b) Connectible curves give causal relations.** Let $x:I\to M$ be a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve and let $t_1<t_2$ in $I$.
Then for every open neighborhood $W$ of $x([t_1,t_2])$ there is a piecewise
smooth future causal curve $\eta:[t_1,t_2]\to W$ with $\eta(t_1)=x(t_1)$ and
$\eta(t_2)=x(t_2)$ (in particular a locally absolutely continuous future
causal curve, so $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$ in the relation defined by
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]).

**(c) Equality of relations.** For $p,q\in M$ the following are equivalent:
$p\le q$; $p=q$ or there is a geodesically connectible continuous causal
curve with endpoints $p,q$.

**(d) One-sided extension.** Let $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ be a
future-inextendible future causal curve in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d). Then there is an
inextendible future causal curve $\gamma^*:I^*\to M$ with
$[0,\infty)\subseteq I^*\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\gamma^*|_{[0,\infty)}=\gamma$;
that is, $\gamma$ is contained in a curve that is both future- and
past-inextendible. The dual statement holds for past-inextendible curves.

No choice principle is used. The extension in (d) is not asserted to be
unique.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: (External structural facts, quoted.) The following published statements about causal and timelike curves as in [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] are used. (i) *Equality of the causal and timelike domains for closed $S$.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be a closed set then $D^+(S)=\widetilde D^+(S)$, $\operatorname{Int}\widetilde D^+(S)=\operatorname{Int}D^+(S)$ and $\dot{\widetilde D^+}(S)=\dot D^+(S)$", the proof establishing that $\widetilde D^+(S)$ is closed; and the achronality identity "If $S$ is achronal, $\widetilde D^+(S)\cap\widetilde D^-(S)=D^+(S)\cap D^-(S)=S$".] (ii) *Openness for partial Cauchy hypersurfaces.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be a partial Cauchy hypersurface, then $D(S)\cap H(S)=\varnothing$, in particular $D(S)$ is open and $H^\pm(S)\subset I^\pm(S)$".] Here $H(S)$ is the Cauchy horizon of $S$, the part of the boundary of the domain of dependence other than $S$; since $D(S)$ is closed ([L1] with [L1]'s equality for the closed set $S$), its boundary contains no point of $D(S)\setminus S$ (else that point would lie in $H(S)$ and in $D(S)$, contradicting $D(S)\cap H(S)=\varnothing$), so $D(S)$ is open around every point of $D(S)\setminus S$; at points of $S$ it is open because the boundary satisfies $\partial D(S)\cap S=\varnothing$: indeed the source's identity $H^\pm(S)\cap S=\mathrm{edge}(S)=\varnothing$ holds as $S$ is edgeless, and $\partial D(S)\setminus S\subseteq H(S)$. (iii) *Causal convexity.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be closed and achronal. The sets $\operatorname{Int}D(S)$, $\operatorname{Int}D^+(S)$ and $\operatorname{Int}D^-(S)$ are all causally convex", i.e. for $p,q\in\operatorname{Int}D(S)$ one has $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)\subseteq\operatorname{Int}D(S)$.] Since $D(S)=\operatorname{Int}D(S)$ by (ii), this is clause (b).

(The chronological-side property, proved from the definition.) Let $p\in D^+(S)\setminus S$. Choose a past-directed timelike geodesic segment $\beta_0:[0,1]\to W$ with $\beta_0(0)=p$ (in a chart at $p$, a small past- directed timelike geodesic exists by the time-orientation, [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). By [L3] let $\beta$ extend $\beta_0$ to a past-directed causal curve in $W$ that is past-inextendible in $W$ with $\beta(0)=p$; passing to the subcurve containing $\beta_0$ keeps the curve timelike on a nondegenerate interval, so $\beta$ is a past-directed past-inextendible **timelike** curve through $p$. Since $p\in D^+(S)$, $\beta$ meets $S$; at some parameter $t_s\le 0$. The subcurve of $\beta$ between $t_s$ and $0$ is a nondegenerate segment of a timelike curve joining $s:=\beta(t_s)\in S$ to $p$; if $s=p$ then $p\in S\cap(D^+(S)\setminus S)=\varnothing$, impossible, so $s\ne p$ and the segment is nondegenerate; by [L2] $s\ll p$, hence $p\in I^+(S)$. The time reverse gives $D^-(S)\setminus S\subseteq I^-(S)$. This proves the "moreover" part of clause (a).

(Disjointness of the chronological sides.) $S$ acausal implies $S$ achronal, and then $I^+(S)\cap I^-(S)=\varnothing$: points $s_1\ll x\ll s_2$ with $s_1,s_2\in S$ give $s_1\ll s_2$ by push-up [L2], contradicting achronality, and conversely every point of the intersection yields such a pair.

(Consequences for curves in $D(S)$.) Let $\gamma:I\to D(S)$ be a causal curve with $\gamma\cap S=\varnothing$. By step 2.1 every value of $\gamma$ lies in $I^+(S)\cup I^-(S)$, which by step 3.1 is a disjoint union of two open sets; by continuity of $\gamma$ on the interval $I$ ([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], [[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) its image is connected, so the image lies entirely in one of the two sides.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, with the
relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$, $J^\pm$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] and the future and past sets of
[[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]]. Then:

**(a) Openness.** For every $x\in M$ the chronological future $I^+(x)$ and
the chronological past $I^-(x)$ are open subsets of $M$.

**(b) The chronological relation is open.** The set
$$\{(x,y)\in M\times M:\ x\ll y\}$$
is open in the product topology of $M\times M$.

**(c) Closure of future and past sets.** Let $F\subseteq M$ be a future set,
that is $I^+(F)\subseteq F$. Then every $q\in\overline F$ satisfies
$I^+(q)\subseteq F$. Dually, if $P$ is a past set ($I^-(P)\subseteq P$) and
$q\in\overline P$, then $I^-(q)\subseteq P$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and the relations $\ll$, $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** if $p\ll q$ and $q\le r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(b)** if $p\le q$ and $q\ll r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(c)** if $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is a future causal curve and there are
$a\le s<t\le b$ such that $\gamma|_{[s,t]}$ is a future timelike curve, then
$\gamma(a)\ll\gamma(b)$;

**(d)** consequently
$$I^+\bigl(J^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega),\qquad I^-\bigl(J^-(\Omega)\bigr)=I^-(\Omega)$$
for every $\Omega\subseteq M$, and dually
$J^+\bigl(I^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega)$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal
classification of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] and the
equivalence of "future-directed" with "pairing negatively with $N$" supplied by
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A **chart
representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ of a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the component map $x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely
continuous on $[a,b]$ in the sense of [[def-absolutely-continuous-function]].
This class does not depend on the chart or on the smooth atlas; that is proved
in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (a).

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point
([[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (c)).

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\in J^+(q)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]).
Call a map $x:I\to M$ a **geodesically connectible continuous causal curve**
when it is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]) and for every strictly convex
normal ball $C$ as produced by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]]
([[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b)) and all
$t_1<t_2$ in $I$ with $x([t_1,t_2])\subseteq C$, the endpoints $x(t_1)$ and
$x(t_2)$ are joined by a future causal geodesic whose image is contained in
$C$. Write $\le$ for the causal relation of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] (defined by locally absolutely
continuous future causal curves) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat .$$

**(a) Absolutely continuous implies connectible.** Every future causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ in the sense of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve.

**(b) Connectible curves give causal relations.** Let $x:I\to M$ be a
geodesically connectible continuous causal curve and let $t_1<t_2$ in $I$.
Then for every open neighborhood $W$ of $x([t_1,t_2])$ there is a piecewise
smooth future causal curve $\eta:[t_1,t_2]\to W$ with $\eta(t_1)=x(t_1)$ and
$\eta(t_2)=x(t_2)$ (in particular a locally absolutely continuous future
causal curve, so $x(t_1)\le x(t_2)$ in the relation defined by
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]).

**(c) Equality of relations.** For $p,q\in M$ the following are equivalent:
$p\le q$; $p=q$ or there is a geodesically connectible continuous causal
curve with endpoints $p,q$.

**(d) One-sided extension.** Let $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ be a
future-inextendible future causal curve in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d). Then there is an
inextendible future causal curve $\gamma^*:I^*\to M$ with
$[0,\infty)\subseteq I^*\subseteq\mathbb R$ and $\gamma^*|_{[0,\infty)}=\gamma$;
that is, $\gamma$ is contained in a curve that is both future- and
past-inextendible. The dual statement holds for past-inextendible curves.

No choice principle is used. The extension in (d) is not asserted to be
unique.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

For the absolutely continuous curve conclusion (c), assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) as required by the cited causal-curve calculus and fundamental theorem. The other clauses use the given smooth observer structure, pointwise adapted-chart existence and finite compactness arguments, without these additional curve-calculus premises. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), and put $n=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$. Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. In a chart $(U,x)$ put $v^a=dx^a(v)$, $v_s=(v^1,v^2,v^3)$ and $|v|_{\mathrm e}=(\sum_{a=0}^3(v^a)^2)^{1/2}$.

**(a) Adapted orthonormal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there are a chart $(U,x)$, $x(p)=0$, a radius $r>0$ with $U=x^{-1}(B_r)$, and $K\ge1$, such that on all of $U$
$$n=\partial_{x^0},\qquad g_{00}\equiv-1,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}.$$

**(b) Cone domination.** The chart and radius in (a) can be chosen so every nonzero future causal vector at any point of $U$ satisfies
$$|v_s|\le K v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le K v^0\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad v^0\ge K^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$

**(c) Curve form.** Every future causal curve $\gamma:I\to U$ of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] has strictly increasing time coordinate, and for all $s<t$ in $I$
$$x^0(\gamma(s))<x^0(\gamma(t)),\qquad |x_s(\gamma(t))-x_s(\gamma(s))|\le K\left(x^0(\gamma(t))-x^0(\gamma(s))\right).$$
Consequently every spatial component satisfies the same bound, and the curve image is the graph of a $K$-Lipschitz function into Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ over the interval $x^0(\gamma(I))$.

**(d) Flat minorant cone.** The same chart can be chosen so the constant-coordinate metric $\eta_{16}=-(dx^0)^2+16\sum_i(dx^i)^2$ has every nonzero $\eta_{16}$-causal vector $g$-timelike throughout $U$. If $q,q'\in U$ and $\eta_{16}(x(q')-x(q),x(q')-x(q))<0$, then $q\ll q'$ if $x^0(q')>x^0(q)$, and $q'\ll q$ otherwise.

**(e) General temporal charts: exact compact uniformity.** For any chart $(U',z)$ define its temporal locus
$$P=\{q\in U':\nabla z^0(q)\text{ is past timelike}\}.$$
For every compact set $K_0\subset P$ there is $L\ge1$ such that all nonzero future causal vectors based in $K_0$, with coordinate components and Euclidean norm taken in $z$, satisfy
$$|v_s|\le L v^0,\qquad |v^i|\le L v^0,\qquad v^0\ge L^{-1}|v|_{\mathrm e}>0.$$
In particular these bounds hold throughout any relatively compact $U_0\Subset U'$ whose closure is contained in $P$, equivalently whose time gradient is past timelike on its entire closure. Timelikeness merely on $U_0$ gives local bounds at each point and uniform bounds on each compact subset of $U_0$; it does not alone give a uniform bound on all of $U_0$.

No additional choice is used to select the pointwise linear bases or compact cone constants. Countable and Dependent Choice are explicitly required only for the general absolutely continuous curve clause (c), through its actual calculus suppliers.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, with the
relations $\ll$, $\le$ and the sets $I^\pm$, $J^\pm$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] and the future and past sets of
[[def-gr-future-and-past-sets]]. Then:

**(a) Openness.** For every $x\in M$ the chronological future $I^+(x)$ and
the chronological past $I^-(x)$ are open subsets of $M$.

**(b) The chronological relation is open.** The set
$$\{(x,y)\in M\times M:\ x\ll y\}$$
is open in the product topology of $M\times M$.

**(c) Closure of future and past sets.** Let $F\subseteq M$ be a future set,
that is $I^+(F)\subseteq F$. Then every $q\in\overline F$ satisfies
$I^+(q)\subseteq F$. Dually, if $P$ is a past set ($I^-(P)\subseteq P$) and
$q\in\overline P$, then $I^-(q)\subseteq P$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ and the relations $\ll$, $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Then:

**(a)** if $p\ll q$ and $q\le r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(b)** if $p\le q$ and $q\ll r$, then $p\ll r$;

**(c)** if $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is a future causal curve and there are
$a\le s<t\le b$ such that $\gamma|_{[s,t]}$ is a future timelike curve, then
$\gamma(a)\ll\gamma(b)$;

**(d)** consequently
$$I^+\bigl(J^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega),\qquad I^-\bigl(J^-(\Omega)\bigr)=I^-(\Omega)$$
for every $\Omega\subseteq M$, and dually
$J^+\bigl(I^+(\Omega)\bigr)=I^+(\Omega)$.

No choice principle is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian
four-manifold ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and put
$$n:=\frac{N}{\sqrt{-g(N,N)}}\quad\text{(pointwise)},\qquad h:=g+2\,n^\flat\otimes n^\flat,$$
with the flat map $\flat$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],
so that $h$ is a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Then:

**(a)** $h$ is a smooth Riemannian (positive definite) metric on $M$.

**(b)** There is a smooth nonnegative proper function $f:M\to[0,\infty)$ such
that the metric
$$h':=(1+|df|_h^2)\,h$$
is a smooth Riemannian metric with $|df|_{h'}\le1$ everywhere.

**(c)** For each connected component $M_0$ of $M$, the metric space
$(M_0,d_{h'})$ is complete, where $d_{h'}$ is the Riemannian distance of
$h'|_{M_0}$ ([[def-riemannian-distance-on-a-connected-manifold]],
[[thm-riemannian-distance-is-a-metric]]).

**(d)** Consequently, for every connected component $M_0$, every subset of
$M_0$ that is closed in $M_0$ and bounded in $d_{h'}$ is compact, and every
closed ball $\{q\in M_0:d_{h'}(q,p)\le r\}$ is compact.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $h$ be a smooth positive
definite metric on $M$ such that $(M,d_h)$ is complete in each connected
component and every closed $d_h$-bounded subset is compact (both hold for the
metric $h'$ of [[thm-gr-auxiliary-complete-riemannian-metric]]).

**(a) Compact parameter intervals.** Let $T>0$ and let
$\alpha_k:[0,T]\to M$ be future causal curves
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]) parametrized by $h$-arclength,
$\ell_h(\alpha_k|_{[s,t]})=t-s$ for all $0\le s\le t\le T$, with
$\alpha_k(0)\to p\in M$. Then some subsequence (still written $\alpha_k$)
converges uniformly in $d_h$ on $[0,T]$ to a map
$\alpha:[0,T]\to M$ with:

**(a1)** $\alpha(0)=p$ and $d_h(\alpha(s),\alpha(t))\le|t-s|$ for all
$s,t\in[0,T]$;

**(a2)** $\alpha$ is a geodesically connectible continuous causal curve in
the sense of [[lem-gr-causal-curve-conventions]];

**(a3)** $\alpha$ is a future causal curve in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]; and for every chart $U$ of the
kind produced by [[lem-gr-dominating-cone-bounds]] clauses (a) and (b), with
domination constant $K$ and time coordinate $x^0$, there is a constant
$C\ge1$, depending only on the chart and $h$, such that
$$t-s\le C\bigl(x^0(\alpha(t))-x^0(\alpha(s))\bigr)$$
whenever $s<t$ and $\alpha([s,t])\subseteq U$;

**(a4)** $\alpha$ is not constant on any nondegenerate parameter interval.

**(b) Half-lines.** Let $\gamma_k:I_k\to M$ be future causal curves
parametrized by $h$-arclength whose intervals $I_k\ni0$ satisfy
$[0,n]\subseteq I_k$ for every $k$ once $n$ is fixed (for instance
$I_k=[0,b_k]$ with $b_k\to\infty$), and suppose $\gamma_k(0)\to p$. Then
some subsequence converges uniformly in $d_h$ on every compact subinterval of
$[0,\infty)$ to a future causal curve $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ satisfying
(a1)-(a4) on compact subintervals and which is future-inextendible
([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (d)). A dual statement
holds, in the time-reversed orientation, for curves whose intervals satisfy
$[-n,0]\subseteq I_k$ eventually; it produces a past-inextendible future
causal curve on $(-\infty,0]$ in the original orientation.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(M,g,N)$ be a
time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with the causal-curve class of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Chart independence.** Local absolute continuity in the sense of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (a) is independent of the
chosen chart and of the smooth atlas: if one chart representative of a curve
is absolutely continuous on every compact parameter subinterval, then so is
every other one.

**(b) Velocity and smooth composition.** At every interior parameter value
$t$ at which one chart representative is differentiable, every chart
representative is differentiable, the velocity $\gamma'(t)$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] clause (b) is well defined and
independent of the chart, and the set of parameter values at which some
chart representative is differentiable has full measure in the domain. For
every smooth map $F$ of an open subset of $M$ into $M$ whose domain contains
the image of $\gamma$, the composite $F\circ\gamma$ is locally absolutely
continuous and $(F\circ\gamma)'(t)=dF_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t))$ at almost
every parameter value $t$.

**(c) Piecewise $C^1$ curves.** Every piecewise $C^1$ curve (in the
one-sided-tangent convention of
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) is locally absolutely
continuous; a piecewise $C^1$ curve all of whose tangents are future causal
is a future causal curve, and if in addition its tangents are future
timelike, it is a future timelike curve.

**(d) Concatenation.** If $\gamma_1:[a,b]\to M$ and $\gamma_2:[b,c]\to M$ are
future causal curves (respectively future timelike curves) with
$\gamma_1(b)=\gamma_2(b)$, then the concatenation $\gamma:[a,c]\to M$,
$\gamma(t):=\gamma_1(t)$ for $t\le b$ and $\gamma(t):=\gamma_2(t)$ for
$t\ge b$, is a future causal (respectively future timelike) curve; the same
holds for any finite chain of such curves.

**(e) Reparametrization.** If $\varphi:J\to I$ is a strictly increasing
$C^1$ diffeomorphism of intervals with $\varphi'>0$ and $\gamma:I\to M$ is
locally absolutely continuous, then $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is locally
absolutely continuous and $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is future causal (respectively
future timelike) exactly when $\gamma$ is. Moreover $\gamma$ is
future-inextendible if and only if $\gamma\circ\varphi$ is
future-inextendible, and this equivalence holds for every strictly increasing
continuous surjection $\varphi$ of intervals, not only the $C^1$ ones.

**(f) Relations.** The relation $\le$ of
[[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] is reflexive and transitive, and
$p\ll q$ implies $p\le q$ for all $p,q$; the relations $J^{\pm}$ and
$I^{\pm}$ of that definition are therefore nested, $I^{\pm}(S)\subseteq
J^{\pm}(S)$ for every $S\subseteq M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let causal
curves be those of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

**(a) Convergent ends are extendible.** Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]) for the general absolutely continuous endpoint argument in this clause. Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a future
causal curve and suppose $b:=\sup I<\infty$ and $\gamma(t)\to x\in M$ as
$t\to\sup I$. Then there is $\varepsilon>0$ and a future causal curve
$\tilde\gamma$ defined on $I\cup[b,b+\varepsilon)$ whose restriction to $I$
is $\gamma$. Consequently a future-inextendible causal curve whose domain is
bounded above does not converge at its upper end, and the dual statement
holds at the past end.

**(b) Maximal geodesics have no limit.** Let $(p,v)\in TM$ with $v\ne0$ and
let $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ be the unique maximal geodesic with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$, as supplied by
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (a). Then
$\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ does not converge to any point of $M$ as $t\to\sup I_{p,v}$
or as $t\to\inf I_{p,v}$ (where convergence at an infinite end means
convergence as $t\to+\infty$ or $t\to-\infty$ respectively).

**(c) Segments lie on inextendible causal curves.** Let $\gamma:[t_0,t_1]\to M$
with $t_0<t_1$ be a future causal curve, or a past causal curve. Then there
is an inextendible causal curve $\hat\gamma:J\to M$ (same direction as
$\gamma$ in the case at hand) and a strictly increasing affine map
$\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to J$ with $\hat\gamma\circ\rho=\gamma$. In particular, any
two distinct points $p,q\in M$ with $p\le q$ and $p\ne q$ lie on a common
inextendible causal curve, and likewise for the past relation.

**(d) Cauchy sets are acausal.** Every Cauchy set of
[[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]] clause (c) is acausal in
the sense of clause (b) of that definition.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]) and geodesics as in
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $p\in M$ and let
$O\subseteq M$ be an open neighborhood of $p$. Then there are a chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ and a radius $r>0$ such that
$C:=x^{-1}(B_r)$, $B_r=\{y\in\mathbb R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<r\}$ based at
$0=x(p)$, is contained in $O$ and has the following properties.

**(a) Normal neighborhood of each point.** For every $q\in C$ define
$$W_q:=\bigl\{u\in\mathcal E_q:\ \exp_q(tu)\in C\ \text{for every }t\in[0,1]\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal E_q$ is the exponential domain of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] clause (d). Then $W_q$ is an
open star-shaped neighborhood of $0$ in $T_qM$, and
$\exp_q|_{W_q}:W_q\to C$ is a diffeomorphism onto $C$.

**(b) Unique contained joining segment.** For all $q,q'\in C$ there is
exactly one geodesic segment joining $q$ to $q'$ whose image is contained in
$C$, namely
$$x_{q,q'}:[0,1]\to C,\qquad x_{q,q'}(t)=\exp_q\bigl(t\,v(q,q')\bigr),$$
where $v(q,q')$ is the two-point inverse velocity of
[[lem-gr-joint-exponential-diffeomorphism]] clause (c). For $q\ne q'$ the
points $x_{q,q'}(t)$, $0<t<1$, lie in $C$ strictly inside the coordinate
ball, i.e. $|x(x_{q,q'}(t))|_{\mathrm e}<r$; and $x_{q',q}$ is the time
reverse of $x_{q,q'}$ up to affine reparametrization.

**(c) Strict convexity.** In the terminology of
[[def-gr-normal-neighborhoods-and-position-vectors]] clause (b), $C$ is a
strictly convex normal neighborhood; in particular the position vector
$P(q,q')=d(\exp_q)_{v(q,q')}\bigl(v(q,q')\bigr)$ and the squared
displacement $D^2(q,q')=g_q\bigl(v(q,q'),v(q,q')\bigr)$ are defined for all
$q,q'\in C$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]). Let $p\in M$ and let $C$ be a
strictly convex normal coordinate ball around $p$ as produced by
[[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]], small enough that the exponential
chart
$$u:=\psi\circ\exp_p^{-1}:C\to\mathbb R^4$$
of [[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]] clause (b)
(for a $g_p$-orthonormal basis with $e_0$ future directed) satisfies
$$g(\nabla u^0,\nabla u^0)<0,\qquad g(\nabla u^0,N)>0\qquad\text{on }C;$$
such a choice exists because both inequalities hold at $p$ (where
$\nabla u^0=-\partial_0$) and are open conditions. Write
$v(q):=\exp_p^{-1}(q)$, $P(p,q):=d(\exp_p)_{v(q)}(v(q))$ and
$D_p^2(q):=g_p(v(q),v(q))=\eta(u(q),u(q))$ on $C$, and let $J^+_C(p)$,
$I^+_C(p)$ be the sets of endpoints in $C$ of future causal, respectively
future timelike, curves ([[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]) with
image in $C$ starting at $p$. Then:

**(a) Causal containment.** For every future causal curve
$\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ with $\sigma(0)=p$ and every $t\in[0,1]$: the position
vector $v(\sigma(t))$ is future causal or zero; equivalently
$D_p^2(\sigma(t))\le0$ and $u^0(\sigma(t))\ge0$.

**(b) Cone characterizations.** With $\mathcal C^+$, $\mathcal T^+$,
$\mathcal N^+$ the sets of future causal or zero, future timelike, and
future null nonzero vectors of $\exp_p^{-1}(C)$ respectively,
$$J^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal C^+),\qquad I^+_C(p)=\exp_p(\mathcal T^+),\qquad J^+_C(p)\setminus\bigl(I^+_C(p)\cup\{p\}\bigr)=\exp_p(\mathcal N^+).$$

**(c) Null rigidity.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$, and let $\hat s\in(0,1]$ satisfy: $v(\sigma(\hat s))$ is
future null nonzero and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for every $t\in(0,\hat s]$. Then
there are $v_0\in\mathcal N^+$ and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous
surjection $\varphi:[0,\hat s]\to[0,1]$ with
$\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for $0\le t\le\hat s$.

**(d) Length maximality.** Let $\sigma:[0,1]\to C$ be future causal with
$\sigma(0)=p$. Then
$$L_g(\sigma)\le\sqrt{-D_p^2\bigl(\sigma(1)\bigr)}=\sqrt{-g_p\bigl(v(\sigma(1)),v(\sigma(1))\bigr)} .$$
If moreover $v(\sigma(1))$ is future timelike and $v(\sigma(t))\ne0$ for all
$t\in(0,1]$, then equality holds if and only if there are $v_0$ future
timelike and a nondecreasing absolutely continuous surjection
$\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $\sigma(t)=\exp_p(\varphi(t)v_0)$ for all $t$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
geodesics, their maximal domains $I_{q,v}$ and the exponential maps
$\exp_q$ be those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Fix
$p\in M$. Write $\pi:TM\to M$ for the bundle projection.

**(a) Smoothness of the joint map.** The set
$$\mathcal D:=\{(q,v)\in TM:\ 1\in I_{q,v}\}\subseteq TM$$
is open in $TM$, and the **joint exponential map**
$$\Phi:\mathcal D\longrightarrow M\times M,\qquad \Phi(q,v):=(q,\exp_q v),$$
is smooth.

**(b) Differential at $(p,0)$.** The differential $d\Phi_{(p,0)}$ is an
isomorphism. Explicitly, fix a smooth chart $(U,x)$ around $p$; it induces
the chart $(TU,Tx)$ of $TM$ and the product chart $(U\times U,x\times x)$ of
$M\times M$, and under the induced identifications
$T_{(p,0)}(TM)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ and
$T_{(p,p)}(M\times M)\cong T_pM\oplus T_pM$ one has
$$d\Phi_{(p,0)}(u,w)=(u,\ u+w)\qquad\text{for all }u,w\in T_pM .$$

**(c) Diffeomorphism and two-point inverse.** There are open neighborhoods
$V\subseteq\mathcal D$ of $(p,0)$ and $W\subseteq M\times M$ of $(p,p)$ such
that $\Phi|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Moreover $V$ can be chosen
product-like: there are a chart $(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$, a radius
$r>0$ and a velocity radius $\rho>0$ such that, writing $B_s:=\{y\in\mathbb
R^4:|y|_{\mathrm e}<s\}$,
$$V=\bigl\{(q,v):\ q\in x^{-1}(B_r),\ \text{the coordinate components of }v\text{ in }(TU,Tx)\text{ lie in }B_\rho\bigr\},$$
and there is $s\in(0,r)$ with $x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$.
Consequently the velocity map
$$v:W\longrightarrow TM,\qquad (q,r)\longmapsto v(q,r):=\text{the vector with }(q,v(q,r))\in V,\ \Phi(q,v(q,r))=(q,r),$$
is well defined and smooth, and $\exp_q\bigl(v(q,r)\bigr)=r$ for all
$(q,r)\in W$.

**(d) Lipschitz bound for the two-point inverse.** On every pair
$x^{-1}(B_s)\times x^{-1}(B_s)\subseteq W$ as in (c) there is a constant
$\Lambda\ge 0$ such that, for all $q,r\in x^{-1}(B_s)$,
$$|v(q,r)|_x\le\Lambda\,\bigl|x(q)-x(r)\bigr|_{\mathrm e},$$
where $|v|_x$ denotes the Euclidean norm of the coordinate components of
$v$ and $v(q,q)=0$. In particular $|v(q,r)|_x\le 2\Lambda s$ on this pair.

before.claim: (External structural facts, quoted.) The following published statements about causal and timelike curves as in [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]] are used. (i) *Equality of the causal and timelike domains for closed $S$.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be a closed set then $D^+(S)=\widetilde D^+(S)$, $\operatorname{Int}\widetilde D^+(S)=\operatorname{Int}D^+(S)$ and $\dot{\widetilde D^+}(S)=\dot D^+(S)$", the proof establishing that $\widetilde D^+(S)$ is closed; and the achronality identity "If $S$ is achronal, $\widetilde D^+(S)\cap\widetilde D^-(S)=D^+(S)\cap D^-(S)=S$".] (ii) *Openness for partial Cauchy hypersurfaces.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be a partial Cauchy hypersurface, then $D(S)\cap H(S)=\varnothing$, in particular $D(S)$ is open and $H^\pm(S)\subset I^\pm(S)$".] Here $H(S)$ is the Cauchy horizon of $S$, the part of the boundary of the domain of dependence other than $S$; since $D(S)$ is closed ([L1] with [L1]'s equality for the closed set $S$), its boundary contains no point of $D(S)\setminus S$ (else that point would lie in $H(S)$ and in $D(S)$, contradicting $D(S)\cap H(S)=\varnothing$), so $D(S)$ is open around every point of $D(S)\setminus S$; at points of $S$ it is open because the boundary satisfies $\partial D(S)\cap S=\varnothing$: indeed the source's identity $H^\pm(S)\cap S=\mathrm{edge}(S)=\varnothing$ holds as $S$ is edgeless, and $\partial D(S)\setminus S\subseteq H(S)$. (iii) *Causal convexity.* [Minguzzi, Section 3: "Let $S$ be closed and achronal. The sets $\operatorname{Int}D(S)$, $\operatorname{Int}D^+(S)$ and $\operatorname{Int}D^-(S)$ are all causally convex", i.e. for $p,q\in\operatorname{Int}D(S)$ one has $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)\subseteq\operatorname{Int}D(S)$.] Since $D(S)=\operatorname{Int}D(S)$ by (ii), this is clause (b).

(The chronological-side property, proved from the definition.) Let $p\in D^+(S)\setminus S$. Choose a past-directed timelike geodesic segment $\beta_0:[0,1]\to W$ with $\beta_0(0)=p$ (in a chart at $p$, a small past- directed timelike geodesic exists by the time-orientation, [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). By [L3] let $\beta$ extend $\beta_0$ to a past-directed causal curve in $W$ that is past-inextendible in $W$ with $\beta(0)=p$; passing to the subcurve containing $\beta_0$ keeps the curve timelike on a nondegenerate interval, so $\beta$ is a past-directed past-inextendible **timelike** curve through $p$. Since $p\in D^+(S)$, $\beta$ meets $S$; at some parameter $t_s\le 0$. The subcurve of $\beta$ between $t_s$ and $0$ is a nondegenerate segment of a timelike curve joining $s:=\beta(t_s)\in S$ to $p$; if $s=p$ then $p\in S\cap(D^+(S)\setminus S)=\varnothing$, impossible, so $s\ne p$ and the segment is nondegenerate; by [L2] $s\ll p$, hence $p\in I^+(S)$. The time reverse gives $D^-(S)\setminus S\subseteq I^-(S)$. This proves the "moreover" part of clause (a).

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $(W,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let $S\subseteq W$ be a closed acausal edgeless embedded topological hypersurface of codimension one. Here acausality forbids causal relations between distinct points of $S$ as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]; **edgeless** means that no $s\in S$ has the following property: every open neighborhood $U$ of $s$ admits $a\in I^-_U(s)$, $b\in I^+_U(s)$ and a timelike curve in $U$ from $a$ to $b$ avoiding $S$. All curves and inextendibility use [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]], so an inextendible end has no point limit in the specified ambient manifold. Define the ambient causal domains by
$$D^+(S)=\{p\in W:\text{every past-inextendible causal curve in }W\text{ through }p\text{ meets }S\},$$
$$D^-(S)=\{p\in W:\text{every future-inextendible causal curve in }W\text{ through }p\text{ meets }S\},\qquad D(S)=D^+(S)\cup D^-(S),$$
as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. Then:

**(a)** $D(S)$ is open, contains $S$, and $D^\pm(S)\setminus S\subseteq I^\pm(S)$.

**(b)** Every causal curve in $W$ with endpoints in $D(S)$ lies in $D(S)$.

**(c)** Every causal curve in the induced open submanifold $D(S)$ which is inextendible there meets $S$ at exactly one parameter value. No smoothness or spacelikeness of the topological hypersurface is required.
